steps.observation: You have 300 seconds. Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Here are the key differences between DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) and RNA (ribonucleic acid):

1. Sugar backbone  
   • DNA contains deoxyribose sugar (lacks an –OH group at the 2′ carbon).  
   • RNA contains ribose sugar (has an –OH group at the 2′ carbon).  

2. Nitrogenous bases  
   • DNA uses adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C) and thymine (T).  
   • RNA uses A, G, C and uracil (U) in place of thymine.  

3. Strand structure  
   • DNA is usually double-stranded, forming the famous double helix.  
   • RNA is usually single-stranded and can fold into complex 3D shapes.  

4. Stability  
   • DNA is chemically more stable (better for long-term storage of genetic information).  
   • RNA’s extra hydroxyl (–OH) makes it more prone to hydrolysis (shorter-lived).  

5. Location in the cell  
   • DNA resides mainly in the cell nucleus (and in mitochondria/chloroplasts).  
   • RNA is synthesized in the nucleus but functions throughout the cell (cytoplasm, ribosomes).  

6. Primary roles  
   • DNA stores and transmits hereditary information.  
   • RNA plays diverse roles:  
     – mRNA (messenger RNA) carries genetic instructions to ribosomes.  
     – tRNA (transfer RNA) brings amino acids for protein synthesis.  
     – rRNA (ribosomal RNA) is a structural/functional component of ribosomes.  
     – Other noncoding RNAs regulate gene expression or catalyze reactions (ribozymes).  

7. Occurrence in viruses  
   • Some viruses use DNA genomes (e.g., herpesvirus).  
   • Other viruses use RNA genomes (e.g., influenza, HIV, coronaviruses).  

In summary, DNA’s chemically stable double helix makes it ideal for long-term information storage, whereas RNA’s structural flexibility and reactivity suit it for a variety of roles in gene expression and regulation.
